1.title: Entering the Wormhole
1.explanation: As the Endurance approaches the wormhole, the image of light bending around it gives a visual sense of gravity shaping paths through curved spacetime. The wormhole is hypothetical, but the scene draws on gravity's real effect on light and motion.

2.title: Cooper Watches 23 Years of Messages
2.explanation: After a short stay near Miller's planet, Cooper returns to find that 23 years have passed for people farther from Gargantua. The scene dramatizes general relativity: strong gravity can make clocks at different locations tick at different rates.

3.title: Cooper Watches 23 Years of Messages
3.explanation: The messages reveal that decades passed for Cooper's family while only hours passed on the planet. That contrast is the film's depiction of gravitational time dilation near a massive black hole.

4.title: The Tesseract and Morse Code
4.explanation: The bookshelf lets Cooper see different moments in Murph's room at once and send a message across time. It is a cinematic metaphor for treating time as a dimension of spacetime, rather than a literal model of how spacetime works.

5.title: Enter the Quantum Realm
5.explanation: The characters shrink into a world where familiar distances and objects behave strangely. The scene borrows the scale and uncertainty associated with quantum physics, but the Quantum Realm is a fictional setting, not a scientific visualization.

7.title: Inverted Bullet Scene
7.explanation: The bullet appears to move backward into the gun, illustrating Tenet's fictional reversal of entropy. In real thermodynamics, entropy can decrease locally, but a whole macroscopic object does not reverse its history this way.

8.title: The Electromagnet
8.explanation: The scene identifies the chest device as an electromagnet powered by a battery and says it keeps steel shrapnel away from Tony's heart. It connects electric current to a magnetic field; the miniature power source and medical setup are fictional.

9.title: Trinity Test
9.explanation: The test dramatizes a nuclear fission chain reaction: splitting heavy atomic nuclei releases energy and neutrons that can trigger further fissions. The film recreates the historical test rather than showing a science demonstration.

10.title: A New Mission
10.explanation: Mission Control replaces the failed landing plan with a return trajectory. A rocket burn changes the spacecraft's momentum; after the burn, the craft's motion and lunar gravity carry it along the new path.

11.title: Because of the Black Hole
11.explanation: The crew discusses how Gargantua's gravity shapes the planets and nearby matter. The scene uses a black hole as the dominant gravitational object in the system; its pull at a distance follows the same gravitational rules as any massive body.

12.title: Entering the Wormhole
12.explanation: The Endurance passes through a tunnel-like opening that connects distant regions of space. That is the film's depiction of a traversable wormhole, a mathematical possibility that has not been observed or shown to be physically usable.

14.title: Spock Describes the Supernova
14.explanation: Spock recounts a star exploding as a supernova and the destruction that follows. The scene connects a star's late life to a powerful stellar explosion, though the red-matter black-hole response is science fiction.

16.title: Tidal Wave on Miller's Planet
16.explanation: The crew lands on a planet outside our solar system and encounters enormous waves. This supplies the exoplanet setting; the nearby black hole also makes the planet's orbit central to the story.

16.title: Rich Purnell Maneuver
16.explanation: The team decodes a proposed course change for the Hermes. The maneuver uses orbital mechanics: carefully changing velocity reshapes the spacecraft's path so it can return to Mars.

17.title: Mr. DNA
17.explanation: The park tour presents DNA as the instruction set used to build an organism and shows how scientists in the story reconstruct dinosaur genomes. The cartoon simplifies genetics: real DNA does not provide a complete, easy blueprint for rebuilding an extinct animal.

18.title: CRISPR and Weaponized DNA
18.explanation: Dr. Caldwell says her research used CRISPR and was repurposed to create weaponized DNA. CRISPR can make targeted edits to genetic material; the rapid, whole-animal transformations in the film are fictional.

19.title: Healing Factor
19.explanation: Wolverine's wounds close unusually quickly, turning tissue repair into a visible superpower. It is a fictional exaggeration of cellular regeneration; biological evolution happens across populations over generations, not as an individual's instant healing.

20.title: Carbon Dioxide Filter Emergency
20.explanation: The crew's carbon dioxide rises as the spacecraft's filter supplies run low. The scene links a life-support failure to human physiology: too much CO2 can impair judgment and, at high levels, prevent normal breathing.

21.title: The Real Test
21.explanation: Nathan reveals that Ava has been evaluating Caleb as much as he has been evaluating her. The scene treats AI as a system that can reason about people and adapt its behavior; it does not show the neural-network design inside the machine.

23.title: Successful Fusion Reaction
23.explanation: Octavius's lab announces a successful fusion reaction: light atomic nuclei join and release energy. The self-sustaining tabletop reactor and its containment behavior are fictional.

24.title: Iron Man's Nanotech Suit
24.explanation: The Mark 50 forms armor and tools around Tony from a compact supply of material. It is a cinematic nanotechnology idea; present-day nanomaterials cannot assemble a full responsive suit this way.

25.title: Docking Scene
25.explanation: Cooper uses the spacecraft's engines to match the damaged station's motion and align for docking. The scene makes precise thrust, orientation, and relative velocity part of the action.

25.title: Rocket Boosters Near Gargantua
25.explanation: The crew plans to use two landers as rocket boosters to change the Endurance's path near Gargantua. Rocket propulsion works by expelling mass to produce thrust; the black-hole escape maneuver itself is highly speculative.

26.title: Jake Wakes Up in His Avatar Body
26.explanation: Jake's brain controls a remotely located, engineered body through the Avatar program's neural link. It illustrates a brain-computer interface; the avatar is a biological body rather than a robot.

27.title: Chaos Theory
27.explanation: Ian Malcolm uses a small, unpredictable change to illustrate how a complex system can respond differently to tiny differences in its starting conditions. The scene introduces sensitivity to initial conditions, though it is an analogy rather than a mathematical demonstration.

28.title: Infection Montage
28.explanation: The montage follows people and shared surfaces as the fictional pathogen spreads between locations. It visualizes transmission chains and how many everyday contacts can connect into an epidemic.

30.title: Repeating Events and the Last Revision
30.explanation: Aaron describes repeated trips through the same events and how each attempt changes what happens next. The film builds a causal loop, a story version of a closed timelike curve; such curves remain theoretical in physics.

31.title: A Signal from Outer Space
31.explanation: Scientists detect a structured signal from beyond Earth and investigate whether it came from intelligent life. That search is an astrobiology and SETI question; the scene does not calculate the Drake Equation.

32.title: Hibernation Pods
32.explanation: The crew discusses using hibernation to stretch limited supplies during a long mission. It depicts fictional suspended animation, which is related to cryonics but does not show real vitrification or a proven way to revive frozen people.

33.title: Critical Desalinization Point
33.explanation: The researchers connect fresh meltwater to a threshold change in ocean circulation. Thermohaline currents depend partly on temperature and salinity because both affect seawater density; the film's sudden global freeze is highly exaggerated.

34.title: Erased from Her Memory
34.explanation: The scene reveals that a procedure removed Joel from Clementine's memories. It connects to the idea that memories depend on physical patterns in the brain, but a clean, targeted memory erasure is fictional.
34.movie: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

35.title: Sonar Concept
35.explanation: Lucius describes turning cellphone microphones into a citywide sonar map. The system uses sound reflections to estimate where objects are; the scene does not specify ultrasonic frequencies.

36.title: Asteroid Drilling Scene
36.explanation: The crew drills into a comet to place a nuclear device, showing a fictional attempt to prevent an Earth impact. It connects to planetary defense planning and the difficulty of operating on a fast-moving small body.
